title: Drifting slip stack: a page-rolling word stack finished by positional tables
method: The scribe keeps, for each (section, Currier language) group, a stack of word slips built from the group's training words in the order they were first met, a word met often contributing more slips than one met rarely. A pointer walks that stack a slip or two per page and a tray holds the last 200 slips it passed, so pages near each other in the book draw on nearly the same slips while pages far apart do not. The word written is chosen by where it stands: the opening glyph is read from a fitted table (paragraph-opening line first word, line first word, rest of a paragraph-opening line, mid-line, where the mid-line table is that of the last glyph of the word just written on the line, so a line's words are linked edge to edge and the link breaks at a line break); the scribe then takes a tray slip that BEGINS with that glyph and, at the end of a line, that also ENDS with a glyph the line-final table offers, writing the slip unchanged. When no slip fits, the word is composed glyph by glyph from a 5-glyph chain fitted on the group and backing off to the whole book, then opened and closed by the same tables. A word may instead be copied from the last 16 words of the page and changed in exactly one place, the copy being finished for its position first so a line-final m-word cannot carry its m into the middle of a line. Word length follows the fitted mean length of the position class, and the tables are read at a sharpness of 0.55 so the commoner entry is likelier. Fitted on the practice training pages only, written onto every page of the book in order.
